title: Rethinking Nostalgia
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

paragraphs.text: In 1688, a nineteen-year-old medical student in the Swiss city of Basel gave a name to a condition he had observed among his countrymen serving as soldiers abroad. The young men lost their appetite, slept badly, wept, and in some cases wasted away and died; they recovered, as a rule, only when sent home. Johannes Hofer combined two Greek words, nostos, meaning a return home, and algos, meaning pain, and called the illness 'nostalgia'.

For the next two centuries nostalgia was treated as a disease in the full medical sense. Physicians debated its cause: one proposed that the sudden change in air pressure experienced by mountain people who descended to the plains damaged the brain, and another blamed the constant clanging of cowbells in the Alps. Military commanders took it seriously. It was reported that Swiss soldiers in foreign armies were forbidden to sing or whistle a certain herdsmen's melody, for fear that it would trigger an outbreak. Proposed remedies ranged from opium and leeches to, in the case of one Russian general in the eighteenth century, the threat of burying sufferers alive. During the American Civil War, army doctors recorded several thousand cases of nostalgia, some of them fatal.

By the early twentieth century, nostalgia had moved from the body to the mind. It was no longer a disease of the nerves but a psychological disorder, variously described as a form of depression or as a refusal to grow up, and it was increasingly distinguished from homesickness, the simple longing for a place. Nostalgia came to mean a longing for a time – usually one's own past – and it kept its bad reputation. To be nostalgic was to be unable to cope with the present.

This view was first seriously challenged by researchers at the University of Southampton, in England, from the late 1990s onwards. Constantine Sedikides, a psychologist who had recently moved there from the United States, noticed that he frequently found himself thinking of his former home. A colleague suggested that he might be depressed. Sedikides disagreed: the memories were tinged with sadness, but they left him feeling more optimistic, not less. With his colleague Tim Wildschut, he began to investigate what nostalgia actually consists of and what it does.

The first step was to find out how common it is. Using a questionnaire that has since been translated into many languages, the Southampton group found that most people report feeling nostalgic at least once a week, and that the experience is strikingly similar across cultures. Nostalgic memories nearly always feature the person remembering as the central character, but surrounded by others – family, friends, companions at some significant event such as a wedding or a holiday. They often begin badly and end well. And although people describe the feeling as bittersweet, the sweetness generally outweighs the bitterness.

The second step was to discover what prompts it. Here the results were unexpected. Nostalgia is brought on by music, by smells, and by meeting old friends, as one might predict, but its most reliable trigger turned out to be negative feeling, and loneliness above all. In experiments, volunteers who were made to feel isolated – by being told, for example, that a personality test showed they were likely to end up alone in life – subsequently reported more nostalgia than others. Yet those who were then encouraged to dwell on a nostalgic memory felt more loved and more supported afterwards than those asked to recall an ordinary event. Nostalgia, the researchers concluded, is not the cause of unhappiness, as doctors had assumed for three hundred years, but a response to it: a resource on which the mind draws when its sense of belonging is threatened. Hofer's soldiers were not sick with nostalgia. They were lonely, and nostalgia was what they had to comfort themselves.

Later studies have added curious details. People report more nostalgia in cold rooms than in warm ones, and those who have been thinking nostalgically judge the room they are in to be warmer than others do. None of this means that nostalgia is always harmless. The research concerns personal memories; a shared longing for an idealised national past is a different matter, and one that advertisers and politicians have long known how to exploit. There is also evidence that for habitual worriers, comparing a golden past with an anxious present can make matters worse. But the old picture has been overturned. The backward glance, it now seems, is less a retreat from life than one of the ways in which people gather the strength to continue with it.

items.stem: What are we told about the condition that Hofer named?

options.A: It affected soldiers who were serving far from home.
options.B: It was caused by the poor food given to soldiers.
options.C: It was common among medical students in Basel.
options.D: It could not be cured by any means.

items.stem: The writer refers to cowbells as an example of

options.A: a treatment that was tried on sufferers.
options.B: an explanation that was put forward for the illness.
options.C: a sound that soldiers were forbidden to make.
options.D: something that reminded soldiers of home.

items.stem: How did the understanding of nostalgia change in the early twentieth century?

options.A: It ceased to be regarded as harmful.
options.B: It was treated as the same thing as homesickness.
options.C: It was thought to affect mainly children.
options.D: It was seen as a problem of the mind rather than of the body.

items.stem: What led Sedikides to begin studying nostalgia?

options.A: the findings of a colleague's research
options.B: his work with patients who were suffering from depression
options.C: his own experience after moving to another country
options.D: the results of a questionnaire used in many countries

groups.instruction: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?
groups.limit:
Write
YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer
NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer
NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

items.text: Army doctors in the American Civil War believed that nostalgia could kill.
People from different cultures experience nostalgia in very different ways.
Nostalgic memories typically involve other people as well as the person remembering.
Women feel nostalgic more often than men do.
The finding that loneliness triggers nostalgia was what might have been predicted.
Nostalgia for a nation's past can be used for commercial and political purposes.

groups.instruction: Complete the summary using the list of words, A–H, below.
groups.limit: Write the correct letter, A–H, next to Questions 37–40.
groups.title: What nostalgia does

rows.text: Experiments showed that nostalgia is most reliably produced by {37} emotions, especially loneliness. Volunteers who had been made to feel isolated reported more nostalgia than others; but after concentrating on a nostalgic memory, they felt more {38}. The researchers concluded that nostalgia is a {39} to unhappiness and not its {40}.

questions.explain:
答案是 A。Hofer 觀察到的是 his countrymen serving as soldiers abroad（在國外當兵的同胞）。
陷阱：D 錯在他們 recovered... only when sent home，送回家就會好；C 把「命名的人是醫學生」偷換成「患者是醫學生」；B 的食物文章沒提，沒胃口是症狀不是原因。
questions.quote: a condition he had observed among his countrymen serving as soldiers abroad

questions.explain:
答案是 B。牛鈴出現在 Physicians debated its cause 之後：有一位醫生把病因歸咎於阿爾卑斯山不停的牛鈴聲。
陷阱：C 是很強的干擾項。被禁止的是 sing or whistle a certain herdsmen's melody（唱或吹某首牧人的曲調），不是牛鈴。
questions.quote: another blamed the constant clanging of cowbells in the Alps

questions.explain:
答案是 D。原文 nostalgia had moved from the body to the mind，不再是神經的疾病，而是 a psychological disorder。
陷阱：A 相反，it kept its bad reputation；B 也相反，它 was increasingly distinguished from homesickness；C 把 a refusal to grow up 誤解成只影響小孩。
questions.quote: By the early twentieth century, nostalgia had moved from the body to the mind.

questions.explain:
答案是 C。Sedikides 從美國搬到英國後，noticed that he frequently found himself thinking of his former home，這些回憶讓他更樂觀，於是開始研究。
陷阱：A 的同事只是說他可能憂鬱，並沒有做研究；D 的問卷是研究開始之後才用的工具。
questions.quote: noticed that he frequently found himself thinking of his former home

questions.explain:
答案是 YES。南北戰爭期間，軍醫 recorded several thousand cases of nostalgia, some of them fatal。把死亡病例記在 nostalgia 名下，表示他們認為它會致命。
同義轉換：fatal ＝ could kill。
questions.quote: army doctors recorded several thousand cases of nostalgia, some of them fatal

questions.explain:
答案是 NO。Southampton 的研究發現 the experience is strikingly similar across cultures。
解題關鍵：strikingly similar 與題目的 very different 相反。
questions.quote: the experience is strikingly similar across cultures

questions.explain:
答案是 YES。懷舊的回憶裡，回憶者幾乎都是主角，but surrounded by others：家人、朋友、重要場合的同伴。
同義轉換：nearly always ＝ typically；surrounded by others ＝ involve other people。
questions.quote: Nostalgic memories nearly always feature the person remembering as the central character, but surrounded by others

questions.explain:
答案是 NOT GIVEN。文章說大多數人每週至少懷舊一次，但沒有比較男性和女性。
陷阱：文章比較過的是不同文化、冷熱房間，從頭到尾沒有提到性別。
questions.quote: most people report feeling nostalgic at least once a week

questions.explain:
答案是 NO。作者說 Here the results were unexpected：音樂、氣味、老朋友會引發懷舊是 as one might predict，但最可靠的觸發因素竟然是負面情緒，尤其是孤獨。
陷阱：as one might predict 修飾的是音樂和氣味那一部分，不是孤獨。
questions.quote: its most reliable trigger turned out to be negative feeling, and loneliness above all

questions.explain:
答案是 YES。對理想化的國家過去的共同嚮往，是 one that advertisers and politicians have long known how to exploit。
同義轉換：advertisers and politicians ＝ commercial and political purposes；exploit ＝ be used。
questions.quote: one that advertisers and politicians have long known how to exploit

questions.explain:
答案是 B（negative）。懷舊最可靠的觸發因素是 negative feeling, and loneliness above all。
陷阱：A（positive）是直覺的答案。大家以為愉快的事才會引發懷舊，研究結果卻相反。
questions.quote: its most reliable trigger turned out to be negative feeling, and loneliness above all

questions.explain:
答案是 C（supported）。被鼓勵回想懷舊記憶的人 felt more loved and more supported afterwards。
陷阱：D（depressed）是二十世紀初對懷舊的舊看法，實驗結果正好相反。
questions.quote: felt more loved and more supported afterwards than those asked to recall an ordinary event

questions.explain:
答案是 F（response）。研究者的結論是 Nostalgia... is not the cause of unhappiness... but a response to it。
陷阱：G（cure）意思接近但文章沒有這樣說，而且文法上 cure 後面要接 for，空格後面是 to，只有 response to 搭配得起來。
questions.quote: but a response to it: a resource on which the mind draws when its sense of belonging is threatened

questions.explain:
答案是 E（cause）。原文 is not the cause of unhappiness，這是醫生們三百年來的假設，被研究推翻。
解題關鍵：摘要把 not the cause... but a response 的順序倒過來寫成 a response... and not its cause。
questions.quote: is not the cause of unhappiness, as doctors had assumed for three hundred years
